The bin edges relative to the go cue are added to each trial's go-cue time to give the absolute time window for that trial, and the spikes are binned against those edges directly.\n\nii.\n```python\ngo = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n    rates[r] = np.diff(pos, axis=1)\n```\n\niii. The bin grid is defined once, as 81 edges relative to the go cue, and reused for every trial and session, so every trial has the same 80 timepoints.\n\nii.\n```python\n# trial window relative to the go cue, and bin width, in seconds\nT_START, T_STOP = -2.5, 1.5\nBIN = 0.05\nN_BINS = int(round((T_STOP - T_START) / BIN))             \n\nREL_EDGES = T_START + BIN * np.arange(N_BINS + 1)         \nCENTERS = REL_EDGES[:-1] + BIN / 2                        \n```\n\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\n```\n\niii. What variables in the raw data is `output` *tongue_y_position* derived from?\n\ni. Column 1 (`tongue_y`) is the value; column 2 (`likelihood`) decides whether the tongue is visible in that frame.\n\nii.\n```python\nts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\nt_cam = np.asarray(ts.timestamps)\ndata = ts.data[:]                        # (n_frames, 3) = x, y, likelihood\ny = data[:, 1].copy()\n```\n\niii. Frames with `likelihood < 0.5` are set to NaN, since the tracker still reports a position when the tongue is not protruding. The surviving values are averaged into 50 ms bins across the whole session, and the 40th and 60th percentiles of *those bin means* give two class edges. Each trial's window is then binned the same way and digitised against those edges, giving classes 0/1/2. Bins containing no visible frame are assigned a fourth class, `3` (`'not visible'`).\n\nii.\n```python\nTONGUE_CONF = 0.5                # tracking likelihood for the tongue to count as visible\nTONGUE_PCT = (40, 60)            # per-session percentiles -> 3 visible classes\nTONGUE_HIDDEN = 3                # no visible tongue frame in the bin\n```\n\n```python\ny[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n# bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\ngidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\nedges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n# per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\ncls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\nlo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\nhi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\nfor i in range(len(go)):\n    b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n    m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n    ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n    cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n```\n\niii. The tongue is visible in only ~10% of frames, and when it is retracted the tracker still emits a position, so those frames are discarded rather than averaged in — including them shifts the percentiles and mixes real protrusions with noise. The likelihood value is effectively binary (89% of frames below 0.01, 10.5% at or above 0.99), so the exact threshold does not matter.\n\nPercentiles are taken over the 50 ms bin means rather than raw frames so the edges are defined on the same quantity that gets discretised; taking them over frames instead skews the resulting class balance, because averaging within a bin pulls values toward the center. The 40th/60th split and the per-session scope both follow the instructions. A fourth class is defined for bins with no visible tongue, which is 75% of all bins.\n\n## 8-d. How is `output` *tongue_y_position* aligned with the neural data?\n\ni. This is the one genuinely time-varying output, so it is the only one needing real alignment. The camera timestamps are on the same session-absolute clock as the spikes and the go cues, so each trial's frame range is found by `searchsorted` on the camera timestamps at `go + T_START` and `go + T_STOP`, and frames are assigned to bins by their offset from `go + T_START` — the same go-cue-relative grid used for the firing rates.\n\nii.\n```python\nlo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\nhi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\nfor i in range(len(go)):\n    b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n```\n\niii. The camera timestamps share the global clock with the spikes and events, so no interpolation or offset correction is needed — the same bin grid is applied to both streams, which guarantees bin `k` of the tongue output covers the same interval as bin `k` of the firing rates.\n\nUnlike the spikes, the video is trial-gated: it runs from `trials.start_time` to the trial-end event and is off during the inter-trial interval. On the ~3% of trials where the go cue falls less than 2.5 s after trial start, the leading bins therefore contain no frames at all and fall into the `'not visible'` class.\n\n## 9. How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?\n\ni. Three cases:\n\n- **Session never quality-controlled**: `classification` and `anno_name` are NaN rather than strings. `_text` maps any non-string entry to `''`, the session then has no `'good'` units, and it is dropped.\n- **Trials without spike data**: excluded via `obs_intervals` and `free_water` (see 1-e).\n- **Frames with no tracked tongue**: set to NaN and excluded from the bin mean; a bin left with no valid frame becomes the `'not visible'` class.\n\nii.\n```python\ndef _text(col):\n    \"\"\"Read a text column; non-str entries (unlabelled sessions) become ''.\"\"\"\n    return np.array([x if isinstance(x, str) else '' for x in col[:]])\n```\n\n```python\ngood = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\nif good.size == 0:\n    return None\n```\n\n```python\ny[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n...\nm = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\nok = ~np.isnan(m)\ncls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n```\n\niii. Missing data is handled one of two ways depending on what it means. Where nothing was recorded, the session or trial is excluded, since emitting it would fabricate data — a trial with no spikes would otherwise appear as 4 s of 0 Hz across every unit. Where the measurement legitimately has no value, as with a retracted tongue, it is represented as an explicit category rather than imputed.\n\n## 10-a. What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?\n\ni. Reading each NWB file dominates. The full conversion takes 247 s for 174 sessions, ~1.4 s per session on average, ranging from ~0.7 s to ~4 s roughly with unit count. Within a session the costs are pulling the `spike_times` buffer (up to ~11.5 M doubles) and the tongue tracking array (~680 k x 3), then the per-unit `searchsorted` loop. Pickling the 11.9 GB result takes a further ~40 s.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The work is dominated by I/O and by one binary search per bin edge per unit, both of which scale with the data actually needed. No step was worth optimising further given the 15-minute budget in the instructions.\n\n## 10-b. What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?\n\ni. Two loops remain. The per-unit loop in the neural binning runs one `searchsorted` per unit, but over *all* trials at once — the per-trial dimension is already vectorised by flattening the edge array. The per-trial loop in `tongue_output` bins one trial's frames at a time.\n\nii.\n```python\nedges = (go[:, None] + REL_EDGES[None, :]).ravel()\nfor r, u in enumerate(good):\n    s = allst[starts[u]:offs[u]]\n    pos = np.searchsorted(s, edges).reshape(n_trials, N_BINS + 1)\n```\n\niii. The per-unit loop cannot be collapsed further because each unit has a different number of spikes, so there is no single sorted array to search — this is inherent to the ragged storage. The tongue loop could be vectorised with a global bin index and one `bincount`, but it runs over trials rather than frames and is not a measurable share of runtime, so it was left in the clearer form.\n\n## 10-c. What processing does the code repeat multiple times?\n\ni. Nothing is recomputed. Each NWB file is opened once and every quantity derived from it is computed once. The bin grid (`REL_EDGES`, `CENTERS`) is built once at module level and reused for every trial and session.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. The conversion is a single pass over the files. Because the tongue discretisation edges are per-session rather than global, they can be computed inside that same pass — no second pass over the data is needed to establish them.\n\n## 10-d. What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?\n\ni. None. Every field computed goes into the output.\n\nii. N/A\n\niii. N/A\n\n## 10-e. How is memory usage optimized?\n\ni. Firing rates are stored as `float32` and the outputs as `int8` rather than the default `float64`. Each session is read inside a `with` block so the file handle and its cached arrays are released on exit, and only the per-trial slices are retained. The full neural payload is 11.9 GB; a single session's working arrays are at most ~0.2 GB.\n\nii.\n```python\nrates = np.empty((good.size, n_trials, N_BINS), np.float32)\n```\n\n```python\nout = np.empty((n_trials, len(OUTPUT_NAMES), N_BINS), np.int8)\n```\n\n```python\ninp = np.stack([time_from_tone, photostim], axis=1).astype(np.float32)\n```\n\niii. `float32` halves the largest object in the output relative to `float64` at no cost, since firing rates are multiples of 20 Hz and well within its precision. Peak memory is set by the accumulated result rather than by any single session, so no further streaming was needed.\n#!/usr/bin/env python3\n\"\"\"Convert the Brain-wide Activity Map dataset (DANDI 000363) to the decoder format.\n\n    python -u convert_data.py <outpicklefile> [--full | --sample] [--datadir DIR]\n\"\"\"\n\nimport argparse\nimport glob\nimport os\nimport pickle\nimport re\nimport sys\nimport time\n\nimport numpy as np\nfrom pynwb import NWBHDF5IO\n\n_chen2024_seed = 'x5cidj2hy87s'\nnp.random.seed(sum(ord(c) for c in _chen2024_seed) % 2**31)\n\nHERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))\n# Default only, for running this by hand from manual/chen2024/. NaN where a bin is empty.\"\"\"\n    ok = ~np.isnan(y)\n    tot = np.bincount(idx[ok], weights=y[ok], minlength=n)\n    cnt = np.bincount(idx[ok], minlength=n)\n    with np.errstate(invalid='ignore'):\n        return np.where(cnt > 0, tot / np.maximum(cnt, 1), np.nan)\n\n\ndef tongue_output(nwb, go):\n    \"\"\"Discretise tongue y into (n_trials, N_BINS) classes.\"\"\"\n    ts = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralTimeSeries'].time_series['Camera0_side_TongueTracking']\n    t_cam = np.asarray(ts.timestamps)\n    data = ts.data[:]                        # (n_frames, 3) = x, y, likelihood\n    y = data[:, 1].copy()\n    y[data[:, 2] < TONGUE_CONF] = np.nan     # keep only visible frames\n\n    # bin the whole session on one grid, then take percentiles of the bin means\n    gidx = np.floor((t_cam - t_cam[0]) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n    edges = np.nanpercentile(_bin_mean(gidx, y, int(gidx[-1]) + 1), TONGUE_PCT)\n\n    # per trial, bin the same way and digitise against those edges\n    cls = np.full((len(go), N_BINS), TONGUE_HIDDEN, np.int8)\n    lo = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_START, 'left')\n    hi = np.searchsorted(t_cam, go + T_STOP, 'left')\n    for i in range(len(go)):\n        b = np.floor((t_cam[lo[i]:hi[i]] - (go[i] + T_START)) / BIN).astype(np.int64)\n        np.clip(b, 0, N_BINS - 1, out=b)\n        m = _bin_mean(b, y[lo[i]:hi[i]], N_BINS)\n        ok = ~np.isnan(m)\n        cls[i, ok] = np.digitize(m[ok], edges)\n    return cls\n\n\ndef process_session(path):\n    \"\"\"Convert one NWB file. Returns a dict, or None if the session is dropped.\"\"\"\n    with NWBHDF5IO(path, mode='r', load_namespaces=True) as io:\n        nwb = io.read()\n        units = nwb.units\n        trials = nwb.trials.to_dataframe()\n        bev = nwb.acquisition['BehavioralEvents'].time_series\n\n        # ---- units: QC classifier verdict ----------------------------------\n        cls = _text(units['classification'])\n        good = np.flatnonzero(cls == 'good')\n        if good.size == 0:\n            return None\n        regions = [region_label(a) for a in _text(units['anno_name'])[good]]\n\n        # all NWB times are session-absolute seconds\n        go = np.asarray(bev['go_start_times'].timestamps)\n        assert len(go) == len(trials), f'{len(go)} go cues vs {len(trials)} trials'\n\n        # ---- trials filtering ----\n        # spike data\n        # obs_intervals gives one [start, stop] per observed trial, which in some\n        # sessions is fewer than the behavioural trials. \n        # a behavioural trial is observed if its start time is one of the interval starts\n        obs = np.asarray(units['obs_intervals'][good[0]])        \n        keep = np.isin(trials['start_time'].values, obs[:, 0])\n        assert keep.sum() == len(obs), f'{keep.sum()} matched vs {len(obs)} observed'\n\n        # filter no water trials\n        keep &= trials['free_water'].values == 0\n        \n        # a sessioon has to have at least 2 trials according to the instruction\n        if keep.sum() < 2:\n            return None\n        \n        trials = trials[keep]\n        go = go[keep]\n        n_trials = len(go)\n\n        # last tone onset before the go cue; The relevant modules:\n\n### Key Functions Identified\n| Function | File | Stage | Purpose |\n|----------|------|-------|---------|\n| `process_all_sess_parallel` / `process_one_sess` | `VideoAnalysisUtils/preprocessing_DJ_2022Aug.py` | LOADING | Top-level ephys preprocessing: concatenates all probes of a session, reads behaviour/task variables, applies QC, splits into regions, writes per-region pickles |\n| `sliding_histogram` | `VideoAnalysisUtils/preprocessing_DJ_2022Aug.py` | PROCESSING | Bins spike times into **firing rates** (`counts / bin_width`) on sliding bins; 174 files)\n| Statistic | Value |\n|-----------|-------|\n| Neurons (total, `classification == 'good'`) | 69,453 |\n| Neurons (total, all Kilosort clusters) | 272,227 (good fraction 25.5 %) |\n| Neurons / session (good) | median 390, mean 399 |\n| Subjects | 28 |\n| Sessions / subject | 3–10 (mean 6.2) |\n| Trials (total) | 94,990 |\n| Trials / session | mean 546, range 264–800 |\n| Outcome fractions | hit 0.687, miss 0.165, ignore 0.148 |\n| Early-lick fraction | 0.114 |\n| Photostimulation fraction | 0.196 (168/174 sessions have photostim) |\n| Instruction fractions | left 0.485, right 0.515 |\n| Auto-water trials | 1,339 (1.4 %) |\n| Free-water trials | 2,450 (2.6 %) |\n| Video streams | all 174 sessions have `Camera0_side_TongueTracking` |\n| Video sampling | 300 Hz, dt = 0.0034 s, session-time timestamps, one contiguous segment per trial |\n\nObservations that drive the conversion:\n1. **Spikes only exist inside `[trial.start_time, trial.stop_time]`.**\n   `go - start_time` ≥ 2.11 s (3.1 % of trials < 2.5 s);\n   `stop_time - go` has a bimodal distribution — ~1.75 s for hit trials, ~1.8 s for\n   ignore trials, but only ~0.2–0.5 s for **miss (error)** trials, because an error\n   lick triggers a timeout and the exported trial ends at the last lick.\n   Consequence: for 15.6 % of trials the [-2.5, +1.5] s window extends beyond the\n   observed interval, and those bins necessarily contain 0 spikes. This is a\n   property of the published dataset, not of this conversion (verified: 100 % of\n   spike times lie inside the trial intervals).\n2. Go-cue times are ≥ 4.58 s apart everywhere, so the 4 s trial windows never overlap.\n3. Every session has exactly one go cue per trial, and at least one sample-epoch\n   onset before each go cue.\n4. `units/is_good_trials` is `True` for 99.88 % of (good unit, trial) pairs, and\n   99.88 % of good units are valid on *all* trials — negligible.\n5. All good units have a non-empty `anno_name` and a non-NaN CCF coordinate.\n\n---\n\n## Step 3: Reference Text Reading\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Expected Statistics (from papers/methods)\n| Statistic | Value | Source Quote |\n|-----------|-------|--------------|\n| Subjects | 28 | \"data from 28 mice\" (methodpaper Methods); the reference\n  extracts [-3, +3] s (ephys) and [-3, +1.5] s (video markers).\n- **Binning**: firing rate = spike count / bin width (Hz).\n- **Video**: DeepLabCut markers for tongue, jaw, nose from the *side* view only.\n  Outliers identified by a five-sigma velocity threshold and imputed from nearby\n  frames. \"When the tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically\n  the case before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean value.\"\n\n### Curation Steps\n\n**Neuron curation rules** (reference):\n- Kilosort2 clusters passing the region-specific logistic-regression QC classifier\n  (\"good\" units). ⇒ NWB `units/classification == 'good'`.\n- Units must have both ephys and histology (i.e. a CCF annotation).\n- For the *single-neuron variance-explained* analyses only: neurons with mean firing\n  rate < 2 Hz excluded, and neurons with R² < 0.01 excluded.\n- `check_fr`: neurons with zero across-trial variance dropped.\n\n**Trial curation rules** (reference):\n- Session selection (datapaper): overall behavioral performance > 65 % **and** at\n  least 50 correct lick-left and 50 correct lick-right trials.\n  Performance = fraction correct among control (no-photostim) trials, excluding\n  early-lick trials.\n- Trial selection (both papers / `get_regular_trial_mask`): exclude photostimulation,\n  free-water, auto-water, early-lick and no-response (\"ignore\") trials.\n\n### Decoders Trained\nThe two reference papers do not train the decoder specified here, so there is no\ndirectly comparable accuracy. The closest reported numbers:\n\n| Decoded variable | Reported performance | Source |\n|---|---|---|\n| Lick direction (choice) from single-neuron delay firing rate | AUC > 0.65 used as the \"choice-modulated\" threshold; population CD<sub>choice</sub> decoding well above chance | methodpaper Fig. 7; datapaper Fig. 4 |\n| Trial type (video-prediction group) from single neurons | AUC > 0.6 / 0.65 thresholds | methodpaper Fig. 6–7 |\n| Behaviour (video) predicted from neural activity | population decoding accuracy ≫ chance | datapaper Fig. 6 |\nNeural-activity-from-video prediction is reported as R² (≈ 0.2–0.8 for the best\nneurons), which is not comparable to classification accuracy.\n\nBecause choice, outcome and (especially) tongue position are strongly represented\nbrain-wide in this dataset, well above-chance decoding is expected for all four\noutputs; tongue position and choice should be the easiest.\n\n---\n\n## Step 4: Check for Consistency\n**Status**: COMPLETE\n\n### Reference `.mat` variable → NWB variable mapping\n| Reference `.mat` variable | NWB equivalent | Check |\n|---|---|---|\n| `task_cue_time[0]` (go cue) | `acquisition/BehavioralEvents/go_start_times/timestamps` | exactly n_trials per session, one per trial, in order ✓ |\n| `task_sample_time` | `sample_start_times` / `sample_stop_times` | duration 0.65 s ✓ |\n| `task_delay_time` | `delay_start_times` / `delay_stop_times` | duration 1.2 s ✓ |\n| `behavior_early_report` | `intervals/trials/early_lick` | |\n| `behavior_is_auto_water`, `behavior_is_free_water` | `auto_water`, `free_water` | |\n| `behavior_report` (1 correct / 0 error / −1 no response) | `outcome` (`hit` / `miss` / `ignore`) | |\n| `task_trial_type` ('l'/'r') | `trial_instruction` (`left`/`right`) | |\n| `behavior_lick_directions`, `behavior_lick_times` | `left_lick_times`, `right_lick_times` | |\n| `task_stimulation` (power, type, on, off) | `photostim_power`, `photostim_onset`, `photostim_duration`, `photostim_start/stop_times` | onset field == event time − trial start ✓ |\n| `neuron_single_units` | `units/spike_times` (+ `spike_times_index`) | |\n| QC `goodunits` index list | `units/classification == 'good'` | good fraction 25.5 % vs 25.9 % reported ✓ |\n| `histology.annotation` | `units/anno_name` | |\n| `histology.ccf_x/y/z` | `electrodes.x/y/z` via `units/electrodes` | x∈[3100,8000] µm, midline 5700 ✓ |\n| `tracking.camera_0_side.tongue_x/y/likelihood` | `Camera0_side_TongueTracking/data[:, 0/1/2]` | |\n\n### Discrepancies Found\n| Topic | Code says | Data shows | Papers say | Resolution |\n|-------|-----------|------------|------------|------------|\n| Number of sessions | n/a | 174 NWB files | \"173 behavioral sessions\" | 174 files, 28 subjects; It is in the file `/app/datapaper.pdf`\\n  - A recent paper that uses this dataset is \\\"Brain-wide analysis reveals movement encoding structured across and within brain areas\\\". It is in the file `/app/methodpaper.pdf`\\n  - A white paper about spike sorting and quality control is in the file `/app/ChenLiuEtAl2023_SpikeSortingQC.pdf`\\n- Some parts of the paper that describe the experiment and processing have been copied to the file `/app/methods.txt`. \\n- **Code**:\\n  - `/app/code` contains code from `/app/methodpaper.pdf`.\\n- **Data** from the papers are in the directory `/app/data`.\\n- **Documentation** on the NWB file format is at https://nwb-schema.readthedocs.io. \\n\\n## Decoder Task\\n\\n- Temporally align based on **Go cue onset**. \\n- Extract **2.5 s before to 1.5 s after** the go cue for each trial\\n- Use **50-ms-width bins** for computing firing rates. \\n\\n### Decoder Inputs:\\n- Time from **tone onset** in seconds (continuous, time-varying)\\n- Whether **photostimulation** is on at every time point (discrete, time-varying)\\n\\n### Decoder Outputs\\n- Lick direction **choice** (left, right, no lick, per-trial)\\n- **Outcome** (ignore, miss, hit, per-trial)\\n- **Early lick** (no, yes, per-trial)\\n- **Tongue y-position**, per-session discretization:\\n  - 0: < 40th percentile of y-position over the session\\n  - 1: 40th to 60th percentile of y-position over the session\\n  - 2: > 60th percentile of y-position over the session\\n  - 3: not visible\\n\\n## Target Data Format\\n\\n- Save the full converted dataset to the pickle file `/app/converted_data.pkl`.\\n- All datasets must be converted into the following Python dictionary structure:\\n\\n```python\\ndata = {\\n    'neural': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # shape: (n_neurons, n_timepoints)\\n            neuron_by_time_matrix,  # trial 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        [  # list of trials for session 2\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'input': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            input_data,  # stimulus/task variables, shape: (n_input, n_timepoints) or (n_input)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'output': [  # list of sessions\\n        [  # list of trials for session 1\\n            output_data,  # behavioral response, shape (n_output, n_timepoints) or (n_output)\\n            ...\\n        ],\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'subjects': list of str, # ids of all subjects, length n_subjects\\n    'subject_idx': shape (n_sessions,), # index into subjects for each session\\n\\n    'brain_regions': list of str, # names of the brain regions recorded from, e.g. ALM, V1\\n    'brain_region_idx': [ # list of sessions\\n        neuron_region_idx, # shape: (n_neurons,)\\n    ], # index into `brain_regions` for each neuron\\n\\n    'input_names': list of str, # names for each input, of length n_input\\n    'output_names': list of str, # names of each output, of length n_output\\n    'output_values': [ # list of length n_output\\n        [ output_val0, ... ], # list of str of length d_output[0], name of each output value\\n        ...\\n    ],\\n\\n    'metadata': {\\n        'task_description': str, # description of output tasks\\n        'time_bin_size': float, # length of time bin in ms\\n        'temporal_alignment_event': str, # description of alignment event\\n        'off_start': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to start of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        'off_end': float or None, # signed time from alignment event to end of trial in seconds, None if N/A\\n        ...\\n    }\\n}\\n```\\n\\n### Key Format Requirements\\n\\n- **neural**: Neural activity data (e.g., firing rates, spike counts) organized by session and trial\\n  - Dimensions: (n_neurons, n_timepoints) for each trial.\\n  - Time bins should be the same size for all trials and sessions. \\n  - There needs to be at least two trials within each session in order to evaluate the decoder performance.\\n\\n- **input**: Variables that serve as inputs **to the decoder**\\n  - These are **decoder inputs**. They could be task inputs to the animal, but inputs to the animal can also be decoder outputs.\\n  - Examples: time from an aligning signal, stimulus characteristics, our animal behavior such as:\\n    - visual: contrast, position, orientation\\n    - audio: frequency, amplitude\\n    - behavior: running speed, pupil size\\n  - Dimensions: (d_input, n_timepoints) for each trial. \\n  - Should capture all relevant contextual information for the decoder\\n  - If an input is a time such as onset of some stimulus, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **output**: Variables to be decoded/predicted from neural activity\\n  - These are what we want the decoder to **predict**. They could be the animal's output behavior or properties of the stimulus.\\n  - Output variables must be **categorical**, i.e. discrete rather than continuous. If a variable is not discrete, follow instructions from Decoder Task to discretize it. \\n  - Examples: stimulus properties (contrast, orientation), choice (left/right), reaction time, position\\n  - Can be time-varying or discrete values per trial. If at all possible, make it time-varying\\n  - If an output is a time such as when a behavior occurred, represent it as a binary time series. \\n\\n- **subjects**: List of names of all unique subjects (mice).\\n- **subject_idx**: Index into subjects for each session.\\n  - Order should match order of sessions in `neural`, etc.\\n\\n- **brain_regions**: List of names of all brain regions recorded from.\\n- **brain_region_idx**: Index into brain_regions for each neuron in each session.\\n\\n- **input_names**: Names of each input variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `input` dimensions. \\n\\n- **output_names**: Names of each output variable.\\n  - Order should match order of `output` dimensions.\\n- **output_values**: Names of each output value for each output variable.\\n  - Order should match categorical `output` values.\\n\\n- **metadata**: Descriptive information. \\n  - `task_description`: Concise description of the task\\n  - `temporal_alignment_event`: Concise description of temporal alignment event\\n  - `off_start`: Signed time from alignment event to start of trial. Negative means before event, positive after. \\n  - `off_end`: Signed time from alignment event to end of trial\\n  - Add other relevant fields, e.g. `session_info`\\n\\n## Python environment\\n\\n- All required Python packages are already installed in the system Python environment.\\n- Use `python3` to run any python code.\\n- If you need to install additional libraries, use `pip install`.\\n\\n## Decoder Reference\\n\\n- Run this script with `python /app/train_decoder.py <data_file_path>` to validate.\\n- Optional arguments:\\n  - `--verify-only`: Only verify data format and print summary, then exit (does not train decoder).\\n  - `--plot-samples`: Plot sample trials from data and save to png files.\\n  - `--cpu`: Force torch to use CPU only (use if GPU runs out of memory).\\n- Pipe the output to the designated file so that the user can examine it.\\n\\n### Purpose\\n\\nThese functions will be used during the validation phase to ensure:\\n1. Data structure is correct - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n2. Dimensions are consistent - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n3. Values are sensible - will report errors and warnings to stdout. \\n4. Decoder can successfully train and predict\\n5. Poor performance indicates data formatting issues that need investigation\\n\\n### Consistency requirements\\n\\nYour processing and formatting must **match the reference papers and code** with respect to:\\n- Loading of data\\n- Temporal alignment of different time series streams (neural, inputs, outputs)\\n- Processing of neural, input, and output data streams\\n- Curation of data: filtering of low-quality neurons, trials, sessions, and mice.\\n\\nTo check consistency, you must compare statistics available in the reference paper and your converted dataset. \\n\\nWhenever possible, invent **SANITY CHECKS** that your loading and processing matches the reference paper and code. \\n\\nDiscrepancies are only allowed if required by the Decoder Input and Decoder Output specifications above, or the task of training a neural decoder.\\n\\nCarefully verify your work after every step. When you find mistakes, document and fix them immediately. Be critical of results **after every step of processing**. \\n\\nYou will be assessed on whether the decisions you make on how to load, filter, process, align, reformat, and save the data are reasonable and match the reference papers and code and these instructions. During testing, the reference version of `/app/train_decoder.py` will be run on your converted data. Data statistics and decoder accuracy will be compared to those achieved by human-written conversion code. \\n\\n---\\n\\n## Conversion Workflow\\n\\n**IMPORTANT**: Follow these steps in order. and video tracking\\n\\nMice performed an auditory delayed response task 21 (Figure 1A). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\n\\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\n\\nPhotoinhibition\\n\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\n\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. This corresponds to 25.9 % of clusters reported by Kilosort2.\\n\\n[stdout]\\n# Setup\\nimport numpy as np\\nimport matplotlib\\nmatplotlib.use('Agg')  # Use non-interactive backend\\nimport and video tracking\\n\\nMice performed an auditory delayed response task 21 (Figure 1A). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. Overall performance was computed as the fraction of correct control trials (i.e. no photostimulation), excluding any early lick trials. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). During the delay epoch, mice maintain a memory of their choice and plan a movement.\\n\\nTwo CMOS cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) were used to track orofacial movements of the mouse under IR light illumination (940 nm LED). The cameras were equipped with 4-12 mm focal length lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron) and a pixel resolution of 71 mm. High-speed videos from a side view and a bottom view (Figure 1C) were acquired at 300 Hz using software FlyCapture (TELEDYNE FLIR). We trained DeepLabCut 39 to track the movement of tongue, jaw and nose (Figure 1I).\\n\\nMulti-regional electrophysiological recordings\\n\\nWe designed a ﬂexible manipulator system for multiple Neuropixels probe insertions (https://www.janelia.org/open-science/manipulator-system-for-multiple-neuropixels-probe-recordings). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. During recordings the craniotomies were immersed in saline.\\n\\nProbes were conﬁgured and data were visualized and streamed to disk using the open-source software package SpikeGLX (https://billkarsh.github.io/SpikeGLX/). Data from up to ﬁve simultaneously recorded probes were acquired at 30 kHz. Sync waves (0.5 s duty cycle TTL pulses) were recorded across probes and on auxiliary channels for synchronization.\\n\\nPhotoinhibition\\n\\nLight from two 473 nm lasers (Coherent OBIS LS/LX) was used to illuminate the two hemispheres of ALM. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). Bilateral ALM photostimulation reduced behavior performance from 83.2% to 71.7% (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice, n = 93 sessions). To exclude the effects of rebound population activity in the thalamus 16 and other subcortical regions, we used a 20-120 ms\\ntime window after photo stimulation onset to measure the effect of ALM inactivation in downstream regions (Figures 5 and S5). For ALM itself, we used 500 ms (i.e. the entire inactivation period) to calculate spike rate reduction.\\n\\nSpike sorting and quality control\\n\\nWe developed a data pipeline for preprocessing, spike sorting and quality control (https://github.com/jenniferColonell/ecephys_spike_sorting). The extracellular recording traces were ﬁrst band-pass ﬁltered (Butterworth acausal ﬁlter, 250 Hz - 9 kHz). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. Each output cluster was associated with a list of 15 quality metrics calculated to assess isolation and sorting quality 7 (i.e. quality control) (https://github.com/AllenInstitute/ecephys_spike_sorting/tree/master/ecephys_spike_sorting/modules/quality_metrics).\\n\\nThe details of the spike sorting and quality control are described in an accompanying white paper (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.v1). In brief, we used 15 cluster quality metrics to train classiﬁers - one for each of the major ﬁve brain areas (cortex, striatum, thalamus, midbrain and medulla). The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. We calculated the rate at which the classiﬁer incorrectly labeled ’unlabeled’ units as ’good’, using 10-fold cross-validation on held-out manually labeled units (false alarm rate): 7.8%; striatum: 6.4%; thalamus: 7.3%; midbrain: 5.5%; medulla 4.3%. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. Licking early during the sample/delay epoch triggered a replay of the epoch. During the response epoch (answer period: 1.5 s) mice reported the instruction by licking one of the two lick ports. Licking (consumption period: 1.5 s) the correct lick port triggered a small water reward (0.1 ~ 0.2 ul). Licking the incorrect lick port triggered a timeout (1-3 s). After mice stopped licking for 1.5 s, the trial ended, followed by a 250 ms inter-trial-interval. Early lick trials and no\\nresponse trials were excluded for analysis. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). The instruction stimuli during the sample epoch were pure tones played at one of two frequencies (3 kHz or 12 kHz). Each tone was played three times for 150 ms with 100 ms inter-tone intervals. The sample epoch was followed by a 1.2 s delay epoch. An auditory ‘Go’ cue (carrier frequency of 6 kHz with 360 Hz modulating fre-\\nquency, 0.1 s duration) indicated the end of the delay epoch. We selected experimental sessions for analysis based on following criteria: overall behavioral performance (> 65%), and at least 50 correct lick left and lick right trials each. Mice performed on average 476 (Mean; range, 130-785) trials per session with 84% correct rate (range, 65-99%; STAR Methods). Three to four small craniotomies (diameter, 1 \\u0018 1.5 mm) were made over target brain areas one day before the ﬁrst recording session. Details of recordings made with multiple Neuropixels probes in head-restrained behaving animals have been published (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.8tphwmn). Target regions, insertions angles, probe types, etc. are summarized in Table S2. All coordinates are given with respect to Bregma (AP, anterior-posterior; ML, medial-lateral; DV, dorsal-ventral).\\n\\nExtracellular spikes were recorded using Neuropixels 1.0 probes, 2.0 single-shank (SS) and 2.0 multi-shank (MS) probes 3,4 (Table S2). Three to seven recordings were made from each craniotomy. Recording depth was inferred from manipulator readings (Sensapax uMp manipulators). After completion of probe insertion, brain tissue was allowed to settle for several minutes before recording. The laser power was controlled by analog outputs controlled by a Bpod (Sanworks). Photoinactivation of ALM (centered on AP 2.5 mm; ML 1.5 mm) was performed through clear-skull cap implant11 or via craniotomy by directing the laser over the skull (beam diameter, 1.8 mm at 4 sigma). Photoinhibition of the left-, right-ALM hemisphere, or both hemispheres was deployed on a subset of ~25% randomly interleaved trials 11,21 (N = 17 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice). To prevent the mice from distinguishing photostimulation trials from control rials using visual cues, a ‘masking ﬂash’ (1 ms pulses at 10 Hz) was delivered using 470 nm LEDs in front of the mice throughout the entire trial. For silencing ALM, we stimulated cortical GABAergic neurons in VGAT-ChR2-EYFP mice. We used 40 Hz photostimulation with a sinusoidal temporal proﬁle (5 mW average power per hemisphere) and a 100 ms linear ramping down during the laser offset to reduce rebound neuronal activity. This photo stimulus is expected to silence glutamatergic neurons in all of ALM. 37 We silenced ALM activity during the late delay epoch (last 0.5 s), including the 100 ms ramp-down. Thus, photoinhibition always ended before the ‘Go’ cue.\\n\\nTo analyze the effects of photoinhibition, units with at least 10 photostimulation trials were selected for analysis (Figures 5 and S5). We then sorted the dataset using both Kilosort2 32 (MATLAB version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/KS20_for_preprocessed_data: Release version of KS2 for preprocessed data) and Kilosort2.5 4 (Python version, GitHub - jenniferColonell/pykilosort: [WIP] Python port of Kilosort 2). Both sorting methods gave similar results. In the analyses presented in the paper, we used the output from Kilosort2. The classiﬁers were trained based on labels derived from manual curation. We curated Kilosort2 output (28 penetrations from ﬁve brain areas) using the open-source graphical user interface Phy (GitHub - cortex-lab/phy: phy: interactive visualization and manual spike sorting of large-scale ephys data). Each cluster was labeled as a ‘good’ or ‘unlabeled’ unit. Annotators were blind to location, recording condition and trial type information. Based on the annotated labels of all clusters and associated quality metrics, we trained ﬁve region-speciﬁc classiﬁers using logistic regression. Applying the trained classiﬁers to the rest of the dataset provided lists of units that were labeled as ‘good’ and were used for the analysis in this paper. We applied the cortex classiﬁer to ALM and other cortex, hippocampus, olfactory and cortical subplate units; the striatum classiﬁer to striatum and pallidum units; the thalamus classiﬁer to thalamus and hypothalamus units; the midbrain classiﬁer to midbrain and pons units; the medulla classiﬁer to medulla and cerebellum units. This method yielded 8717 good units from ALM, 7664 from striatum, 12808 from thalamus, 7495 from midbrain and 2928 from medulla, etc. Overall, the dataset consisted of 69,943 good units recorded across 173 behavioral sessions, from which 655 probe insertions were made. This is to deal with cases where for e.g. (bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride is actually 43 but evaluates to 42.999999... due to numerical errors in floating-point arithmetic.\\\\n    if np.allclose((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride, math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1):\\\\n        n_bins =  math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+2\\\\n    else:\\\\n        n_bins = math.floor((bin_end_time-bin_begin_time)/stride)+1\\\\n    binCenters = bin_begin_time + np.arange(n_bins)*stride\\\\n\\\\n    binIntervals = np.vstack((binCenters-bin_width/2, binCenters+bin_width/2)).T\\\\n\\\\n    # This \\nstudy is based on data from 28 mice, including 25 VGAT-ChR2-EYFP (The \\nJackson Laboratory, JAX no. 014548), one C57BL/6J ( JAX no. 000664), \\none Sst-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 013044) crossed with reporter mouse Ai32 \\n( JAX no. 024109) and one Emx1-IRES-Cre ( JAX no. 005628) crossed \\nwith R26-LNL-GtACR1-Fred-Kv2.1 reporter mouse ( JAX no. 033089). \\nThe mice were 3–7 months old at the time of recording. All procedures \\nwere in accordance with protocols approved by the Janelia Research \\nCampus Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee.\\nThe data were obtained from Neuropixels probes33 used to record \\nextracellular activity in multiple regions of the mouse brain. T o perform \\nspike-sorting, we used Kilosort56 with a custom quality control pipeline \\noutlined in a whitepaper57 (https://doi.org/10.25378/janelia.24066108.\\nv1). We then binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms \\nand a stride of 3.4 ms.\\nIn addition to neural activity, we recorded high-speed (300 Hz) \\nmultiview video of the face, paws and body of the mouse using comple-\\nmentary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) \\nunder infrared (940 nm light emitting diode) light, with 4–12-mm focal \\nlength lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron), achieving a pixel resolution \\nof 71 µm. For analysis, only the side-view frames were used. We used \\nDeepLabCut24 to obtain the positions of the jaw, paws and tongue. We \\nrefer to these positions as markers. We manually labeled about 2,800 \\nframes, and trained the model using this software, and we used the \\nsame model across all sessions. Although these markers were mostly \\nreliable, we found outliers that harmed the prediction of firing rates \\nor animal behavior. We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on \\nvelocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames. When \\nthe tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically the \\ncase before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean \\nvalue. We note that other choices of specific data imputation method \\ndid not qualitatively affect the results.\\nFurther details regarding the animals, behavior and data collec-\\ntion, including electrophysiology, video tracking, spike-sorting and \\nhistology, can be found in ref. 30.\\nConvolutional autoencoder\\nThe architecture of the convolutional autoencoder we used was \\nsimilar to BehaveNet described in ref. 22. The encoder was composed \\nof an initial convolutional layer, two residual blocks 58 and two fully \\nconnected layers. The initial convolutional layer has 3 × 3 kernel size \\nand 16 output channels and is followed by ReLU activation and a 2 × 2 \\nmax pooling. Each residual block was composed of four convolutional \\nlayers. Each convolutional layer has kernel size 3 and stride 1. The \\nfirst residual block had 16 channels; and the second residual block \\nincreased the channel number to 32 in the first layer. Each convolu-\\ntional layer is followed by ReLU activation and the second residual \\nblock ends with a max pooling with kernel size 4. The input image was \\nresized into a 120 × 112 matrix. The output of the last convolutional \\nlayer was a vector with a length of 288. This output was then processed \\nby the two fully connected layers (288 × 128 and 128 × 16) with ReLU \\nactivation between them yielding the output of the encoder, the \\nembedding vector, with a length of 16. The decoder was a fully con-\\nnected linear layer.\\nWe trained and primarily used session-specific autoencoders. \\nHowever, we also verified that one can train a session-independent \\nencoder with session-dependent decoders. We note that decoders had \\nto be session-dependent due to differences in overall position of the \\nmouse, experimental components and background. In other words, \\nduring training, all frames are fed into the same encoder but will then go \\nto different decoders depending on which session they were extracted \\nfrom. We verified that training a session-independent autoencoder \\nwith 40 sessions yielded similar performance and qualitatively similar \\nanalysis results to a session-dependent decoder. We also verified that \\nthe encoder can then generalize to sessions that the encoder has never \\nseen before.\\nEnd-to-end learning framework\\nIn the end-to-end learning framework, we trained deep neural networks \\nto directly predict neural firing rates. For each session with each brain \\nregion, we trained a neural network. The network was composed of \\nthree residual blocks 58 and a final linear output layer. Each residual \\nblock was composed of four convolutional layers, and each convolu-\\ntional layer was followed by a two-dimensional batch normalization \\nwith epsilon 1 × 10−5 and momentum 0.1. The first convolutional layer \\nof a residual block had kernel size 1 and stride 1; the latter three had \\n3 × 3 kernel size and stride 1. The output of the first residual block had \\n16 channels, and the output of the other two blocks had 32 channels. \\nEach residual block was followed by a two-dimensional max pooling \\nwith a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 4 for down sampling. After each \\nbatch normalization or max pooling, a ReLU activation was applied. \\nAfter the three residual blocks and the max poolings, the output was a \\nvector of length 160. A linear output layer was connected to the end of \\nthe last residual block with output size equal to the number of neurons \\nto be predicted in the session.\\nPrediction of neural activity using embedding or markers\\nWhen predicting neural activity at time t  from embedding vectors \\nor marker positions, we took a 5-frame window of the video and col -\\nlected the respective features at t  − 6.8 ms, t − 3.4 ms, t, t + 3.4 ms \\nand t + 6.8 ms and concatenated these vectors, obtaining a single \\nfeature vector that was 80-dimensional for the embedding-based \\napproach (16 latent dimensions times the 5 neighboring time points) \\nand 15-dimensional for the marker-based approach (3 markers \\ntimes the 5 time points). We then used L2 regularized linear regres-\\nsion (ridge-regression) to predict neural activity at time t . The \\nregularization parameter was obtained through fivefold nested \\ncross-validation. Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were \\nexcluded from analyses; the results were not sensitive to the exact \\nvalue of this threshold.\\nTrial selection and cross-validation\\nThe dataset contains trials with photoinhibition, water administration \\nregardless of the animals’ choice (free water trials), early licks and \\ntrials where the animal ignores the lick-spouts. These were excluded \\nfrom all analyses.\\nFor the analyses comparing the three methods (Fig. 2 and Extended \\nData Figs. 2 and 3), we used a single, random train-test split, with balanc-\\ning of the ratio of lick-left, lick-right and correct versus error trials in \\nthe training and test splits. The test split was 64 trials for all sessions, \\nand the same splits were kept across methods.\\nFor analyses involving only the embedding-based meth -\\nods (Figs. 3 –5 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6), we used fivefold \\ncross-validation, stratified with regards to licking direction and cor -\\nrectness across the folds.\\nFor analyses involving behavioral prediction (Figs. 6  and 7 and \\nExtended Data Figs. 7 and 9), we selected only correct trials and used \\n20-fold stratified cross-validation.\\nThalamic nuclei. We then binned spikes into firing rates with a bin width of 40 ms \\nand a stride of 3.4 ms.\\nIn addition to neural activity, we recorded high-speed (300 Hz) \\nmultiview video of the face, paws and body of the mouse using comple-\\nmentary metal-oxide semiconductor cameras (CM3-U3-13Y3M, FLIR) \\nunder infrared (940 nm light emitting diode) light, with 4–12-mm focal \\nlength lenses (12VM412ASIR, Tamron), achieving a pixel resolution \\nof 71 µm. For analysis, only the side-view frames were used. We used \\nDeepLabCut24 to obtain the positions of the jaw, paws and tongue. We \\nrefer to these positions as markers. We manually labeled about 2,800 \\nframes, and trained the model using this software, and we used the \\nsame model across all sessions. Although these markers were mostly \\nreliable, we found outliers that harmed the prediction of firing rates \\nor animal behavior. We identified outliers by a five-sigma threshold on \\nvelocity across frames and imputed outliers from nearby frames. When \\nthe tongue was occluded while it was in the mouth, as was typically the \\ncase before the response epoch, we set the tongue position to its mean \\nvalue. We note that other choices of specific data imputation method \\ndid not qualitatively affect the results.\\nFurther details regarding the animals, behavior and data collec-\\ntion, including electrophysiology, video tracking, spike-sorting and \\nhistology, can be found in ref. 30.\\nConvolutional autoencoder\\nThe architecture of the convolutional autoencoder we used was \\nsimilar to BehaveNet described in ref. 22. The encoder was composed \\nof an initial convolutional layer, two residual blocks 58 and two fully \\nconnected layers. The initial convolutional layer has 3 × 3 kernel size \\nand 16 output channels and is followed by ReLU activation and a 2 × 2 \\nmax pooling. Each residual block was composed of four convolutional \\nlayers. Each convolutional layer has kernel size 3 and stride 1. The \\nfirst residual block had 16 channels; and the second residual block \\nincreased the channel number to 32 in the first layer. Each convolu-\\ntional layer is followed by ReLU activation and the second residual \\nblock ends with a max pooling with kernel size 4. The input image was \\nresized into a 120 × 112 matrix. The output of the last convolutional \\nlayer was a vector with a length of 288. This output was then processed \\nby the two fully connected layers (288 × 128 and 128 × 16) with ReLU \\nactivation between them yielding the output of the encoder, the \\nembedding vector, with a length of 16. The decoder was a fully con-\\nnected linear layer.\\nWe trained and primarily used session-specific autoencoders. \\nHowever, we also verified that one can train a session-independent \\nencoder with session-dependent decoders. We note that decoders had \\nto be session-dependent due to differences in overall position of the \\nmouse, experimental components and background. In other words, \\nduring training, all frames are fed into the same encoder but will then go \\nto different decoders depending on which session they were extracted \\nfrom. We verified that training a session-independent autoencoder \\nwith 40 sessions yielded similar performance and qualitatively similar \\nanalysis results to a session-dependent decoder. We also verified that \\nthe encoder can then generalize to sessions that the encoder has never \\nseen before.\\nEnd-to-end learning framework\\nIn the end-to-end learning framework, we trained deep neural networks \\nto directly predict neural firing rates. For each session with each brain \\nregion, we trained a neural network. The network was composed of \\nthree residual blocks 58 and a final linear output layer. Each residual \\nblock was composed of four convolutional layers, and each convolu-\\ntional layer was followed by a two-dimensional batch normalization \\nwith epsilon 1 × 10−5 and momentum 0.1. The first convolutional layer \\nof a residual block had kernel size 1 and stride 1; the latter three had \\n3 × 3 kernel size and stride 1. The output of the first residual block had \\n16 channels, and the output of the other two blocks had 32 channels. \\nEach residual block was followed by a two-dimensional max pooling \\nwith a kernel size of 4 and a stride of 4 for down sampling. After each \\nbatch normalization or max pooling, a ReLU activation was applied. \\nAfter the three residual blocks and the max poolings, the output was a \\nvector of length 160. A linear output layer was connected to the end of \\nthe last residual block with output size equal to the number of neurons \\nto be predicted in the session.\\nPrediction of neural activity using embedding or markers\\nWhen predicting neural activity at time t  from embedding vectors \\nor marker positions, we took a 5-frame window of the video and col -\\nlected the respective features at t  − 6.8 ms, t − 3.4 ms, t, t + 3.4 ms \\nand t + 6.8 ms and concatenated these vectors, obtaining a single \\nfeature vector that was 80-dimensional for the embedding-based \\napproach (16 latent dimensions times the 5 neighboring time points) \\nand 15-dimensional for the marker-based approach (3 markers \\ntimes the 5 time points). We then used L2 regularized linear regres-\\nsion (ridge-regression) to predict neural activity at time t . The \\nregularization parameter was obtained through fivefold nested \\ncross-validation. Neurons with low firing rates (below 2 Hz) were \\nexcluded from analyses; the results were not sensitive to the exact \\nvalue of this threshold.\\nTrial selection and cross-validation\\nThe dataset contains trials with photoinhibition, water administration \\nregardless of the animals’ choice (free water trials), early licks and \\ntrials where the animal ignores the lick-spouts. These were excluded \\nfrom all analyses.\\nFor the analyses comparing the three methods (Fig. 2 and Extended \\nData Figs. 2 and 3), we used a single, random train-test split, with balanc-\\ning of the ratio of lick-left, lick-right and correct versus error trials in \\nthe training and test splits. The test split was 64 trials for all sessions, \\nand the same splits were kept across methods.\\nFor analyses involving only the embedding-based meth -\\nods (Figs. 3 –5 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6), we used fivefold \\ncross-validation, stratified with regards to licking direction and cor -\\nrectness across the folds.\\nFor analyses involving behavioral prediction (Figs. 6  and 7 and \\nExtended Data Figs. 7 and 9), we selected only correct trials and used \\n20-fold stratified cross-validation.\\nThalamic nuclei. The test split was 64 trials for all sessions, \\nand the same splits were kept across methods.\\nFor analyses involving only the embedding-based meth -\\nods (Figs. 3 –5 and Extended Data Figs. 4–6), we used fivefold \\ncross-validation, stratified with regards to licking direction and cor -\\nrectness across the folds.\\nFor analyses involving behavioral prediction (Figs. 6  and 7 and \\nExtended Data Figs. 7 and 9), we selected only correct trials and used \\n20-fold stratified cross-validation.\\nThalamic nuclei. Then, \\nwe rectified the explained variance scores by setting all negative values \\nto 0. After this, the folds were averaged. The exact value of these \\nthresholds does not change the qualitative type or the approximate \\nproportion of these neurons found in the dataset.\\nAnalyzing optimal time-offsets\\nWhen analyzing the optimal time-shift between video and neural activ-\\nity, we shift the video by tau (τ ) in time (multiples of 6.8 ms which \\ncorresponds to two frames). Then we repeat the same analysis that \\nwe did when predicting neural activity using embedding vectors \\nfor a large set of possible time-shifts (−102 ≤ τ  ≤ 102 ms): we take the \\nfeatures corresponding to five neighboring frames at t  + τ − 6.8 ms, \\nt + τ − 3.4 ms, t + τ, t + τ + 3.4 ms, t + τ + 6.8 ms; predict neural activity \\nusing ridge-regression for every time point separately; and calculate \\nthe epoch-averaged explained variance for each possible τ time-shift. \\nThe optimal time-shift is the one that maximizes the explained \\nvariance τ* = max_τ(R2(τ)). Signifi-\\ncance was established through Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery \\nrate control, with rate parameter Q = 0.05.\\nDefining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated \\nneurons using video-based choice decoder\\nT o define choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons \\n(Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9), we used all correct trials and split them \\ninto four groups based on licking direction and the delay epoch video \\nprediction (obtained as described above). Sessions with fewer than \\n20 trials in any of the four groups were excluded. We used regularized \\nlogistic regression either to predict choice while conditioning for video \\nprediction or to predict uninstructed movement type (video prediction) \\nwhile conditioning for choice from average firing rates of single neurons \\nduring the delay epoch. The prediction was characterized by ROC AUC on \\nthe test-fold and the two conditions were averaged in each case, yielding \\na single AUC for choice prediction and another AUC for uninstructed \\nmovement prediction for each neuron. The final AUC for each neuron \\nis the average of the test AUC across all test-folds. The regularization \\nparameter was found through nested leave-one-out cross-validation.\\nA neuron was then grouped as choice- versus uninstructed \\nmovement-modulated if the relevant AUC exceeded 0.65; note that \\nsome neurons have AUC higher than this threshold for both variables.\\nDefining choice-modulated neurons after subtraction of \\nmovement-related activity\\nT o define neurons modulated by choice but unaffected by any unin-\\nstructed movements (Extended Data Fig. 10), we first subtracted the \\npredicted per-timepoint neural activity based on the embedding \\nmethod of each neuron. We then used regularized logistic regression \\nto predict choice from single-neuron residual activity using fivefold \\ncross-validation, with nested cross-validation to find the regulariza-\\ntion parameter. Each neuron’s choice decoding AUC is the average \\ntest-fold AUC across all cross-validation folds. T o classify a neuron \\nas choice-modulated we used the same threshold as for the other \\nmethod, AUC > 0.65.\\nCalinski–Harabasz clustering score\\nThe Calinski–Harabasz index, also known as the variance ratio criterion, \\nis the ratio of the sum of between-clusters dispersion of a measured \\nfeature to the inter-cluster dispersion for all clusters. Higher scores \\nindicate stronger clustering. T o obtain a reference null-distribution \\nfor the Calinski–Harabasz score, we randomly assign the labels (mice) \\nto each data point, and then calculate the score, repeating the random \\nprocess 1,000 times. We assess significance by comparison to this \\nnull distribution.\\nWe used this clustering score two times. In Fig. 6d, we take the \\nAUC from the embedding framework as features and mouse identity \\nas cluster labels. In Fig. 6e, AUCs from the jaw and the nose markers \\nwere used as features, and mouse identity was used as cluster labels. \\nWe note that we used only sessions where the trial type was predictable \\nfrom either jaw or nose (AUC equal to or higher than 0.65) and only mice \\nthat had two or more of such predictable sessions.\\nTesting against spatial discontinuity with nearest-neighbor \\nexplained variance difference distribution\\nT o test whether spatially closer neurons have smaller difference in their \\nexplained variance than expected by chance within thalamus (Fig. 3e), \\nwe first identified neurons within each nucleus and calculated the \\ncumulative distribution function for the explained variance difference \\nbetween nearest neighbors. As a control we randomly shuffled the \\nneurons’ explained variance values within each nucleus separately and \\ncalculated the cumulative distribution function for the explained vari-\\nance difference in the shuffled sample. We repeated the shuffle 1,000 \\ntimes to establish a null-distribution and bootstrap P value.\\nTest against spatial uniformity\\nT o test against spatial uniformity (Figs. 3 and 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9) \\nof a given scalar statistic (explained variance, single-neuron AUC) \\ngiven the fixed sampling provided by the CCF coordinates, we split \\nthe brain into cubic voxels (0.2 mm cubed for Fig. 3 and 0.5 mm cubed \\nfor Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9, but the results do not depend on \\nthe specific choice of this size) and grouped neurons based on these \\nvoxels. We then calculated an F-statistic for this grouping using one-way \\nF-test. As a control we randomly shuffled the scalar statistics of interest \\n(explained variance, single-neuron AUC) across neurons while keeping \\nthe CCF coordinates fixed; we used the same cubic voxels as before to \\ngroup the shuffled neurons and calculated an F-statistic for this shuffle \\ncontrol using one-way F-test. We repeated the shuffle 10,000 times to \\nestablish a null-distribution and bootstrap P value.\\nData pooling\\nThe registration of individual animals into a common reference frame \\n(CCF v.3) allowed us to pool data across animals when it was neces -\\nsary to combine neurons across animals (Figs. 2a, 3–5 and 7c,d). Higher scores \\nindicate stronger clustering. Neurons were classified into choice- or \\n=== extended/supp ===\\nArticle https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02114-x\\nEpoch-averaged explained variance\\nT o calculate epoch average explained variance we first calculated the \\nexplained variance for each time point and test-fold separately. Then, \\nwe rectified the explained variance scores by setting all negative values \\nto 0. After this, the folds were averaged. Finally, we averaged the time \\npoints within the relevant epoch (sample, delay or response). T o avoid \\nedge effects and compare the same time points (for neural activity) \\nacross all time-shifts, we excluded the first and last 150 ms of each \\nepoch when taking the average. We filtered out neurons with very low \\nexplained variances (below 0.01); the results were not sensitive to the \\nexact value of this threshold.\\nIdentifying neurons with reliable firing patterns and poor \\nvideo prediction\\nT o identify neurons with highly reliable spiking patterns across \\ntrials but poor predictions from behavioral videos (as shown in \\nExtended Data Fig. 1), we selected neurons with low epoch-averaged \\nexplained variance (embedding-based response epoch-explained \\nvariance < 0.1), with high correlation between the single-trial firing \\nrate traces and the trial-averaged firing rate pattern (correlation > 0.4) \\nand with low trial-by-trial variability (average across all time points of \\ninstantaneous trial-to-trial firing rate variance < 100 s−2). We have found \\na total of 196 such neurons in the whole dataset. The exact value of these \\nthresholds does not change the qualitative type or the approximate \\nproportion of these neurons found in the dataset.\\nAnalyzing optimal time-offsets\\nWhen analyzing the optimal time-shift between video and neural activ-\\nity, we shift the video by tau (τ ) in time (multiples of 6.8 ms which \\ncorresponds to two frames). Then we repeat the same analysis that \\nwe did when predicting neural activity using embedding vectors \\nfor a large set of possible time-shifts (−102 ≤ τ  ≤ 102 ms): we take the \\nfeatures corresponding to five neighboring frames at t  + τ − 6.8 ms, \\nt + τ − 3.4 ms, t + τ, t + τ + 3.4 ms, t + τ + 6.8 ms; predict neural activity \\nusing ridge-regression for every time point separately; and calculate \\nthe epoch-averaged explained variance for each possible τ time-shift. \\nThe optimal time-shift is the one that maximizes the explained \\nvariance τ* = max_τ(R2(τ)). Since some neurons’ explained variance \\ncurves as function of time-offset were flat, we kept only neurons with \\nwell-defined peaks (max(R2) ≥ 1.2mean(R2), where mean(R2) is the mean \\nexplained variance across all time-shifts); the results were not sensitive \\nto the exact value of this threshold.\\nT o assess the significance of a neuron’s time-offset (Fig. 5 ), we \\nused the explained variances from the different cross-validation folds \\nand compared the optimal time shifts coming from the different folds \\nagainst zero, using a t-test to obtain a P value for each neuron. Signifi-\\ncance was established through Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery \\nrate control, with rate parameter Q = 0.05.\\nDefining choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated \\nneurons using video-based choice decoder\\nT o define choice- and uninstructed movement-modulated neurons \\n(Fig. 7 and Extended Data Fig. 9), we used all correct trials and split them \\ninto four groups based on licking direction and the delay epoch video \\nprediction (obtained as described above).
